answer:
Use a multi-stage funnel: candidate pools from followed creators, content similarity, collaborative retrieval, and controlled exploration; a ranking stage predicts satisfaction signals; a final layer enforces diversity, safety, and repetition limits. Capture swipe, dwell, completion, replay, explicit feedback, and exposure position with reliable event IDs.

A streaming feature path updates session state after each interaction, allowing the last few swipes to change ranking. Handle event-time ordering, duplicate events, late arrivals, and feature freshness; the request can also carry its latest confirmed actions to bridge stream lag. Keep persistent interests and short-session interests distinct.

Watch time favors longer videos, while completion favors shorter ones. Model multiple outcomes and normalize/segment by length; optimize a validated satisfaction objective with negative-feedback and retention guardrails. Do not interpret every rapid swipe identically. Evaluate session satisfaction, creator diversity, repeats, harmful exposure, and long-term retention. A stale-stream fallback uses durable user features and safe popular candidates rather than blocking the feed.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** A multi-objective score might combine expected satisfaction, completion, and negative-feedback costs, but weights encode product tradeoffs rather than universal constants. Use long-term holdouts to detect novelty effects and feedback loops. Diversity constraints and exploration preserve coverage; training only on previous top-ranked impressions can reinforce a narrow view of user preference. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://engineering.fb.com/2023/08/09/ml-applications/scaling-instagram-explore-recommendations-system/) and [2](https://engineering.fb.com/2026/01/14/ml-applications/adapting-the-facebook-reels-recsys-ai-model-based-on-user-feedback/).
